description: HELIOS is building an immersive 3D experience for exploring NASA’s abandoned hardware in space, from Moon landers to deep-space probes, with the story behind each one. We’re looking for a 3D/graphics developer, 3D artist, data/backend dev, space historian/writer, and designer/video editor. Beginners welcome. Well-organised team, clear scope, and a friendly Discord. Join us and make something people will remember.
summary:
We developed Chronicles of the Silent Pioneers , an interactive 3D web-comic and hardware lab built for school-age learners. Addressing NASA’s "Abandoned but Not Forgotten" challenge, it brings retired equipment on the Moon and Mars—Opportunity & Spirit, the Apollo 11 Descent Stage, and Ingenuity—to life through storytelling and hands-on science.
Users begin on a 3D orbital globe marked with exact NASA resting coordinates, explore graphic-novel issues that clearly distinguish dramatized speech balloons from documented history, and inspect interactive 3D hardware models. Instead of passively reading trivia, students operate the machines themselves through 15-second Spectrometer Scans for Martian water minerals, Signal Delay rover driving simulations, and unlockable mastery badges.
This project is important because young learners often overlook left-behind spacecraft as dead space trash. By turning every broken wheel, dust-covered solar panel, and discarded lander stage into a playable story of engineering sacrifice and scientific discovery, our multilingual, audio-supported experience sparks lasting curiosity and personal connection to human space exploration.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Chronicles of the Silent Pioneers (https://helios-space-apps-2026.vercel.app) is a browser-based motion comic app that turns retired NASA equipment on the Moon and Mars into interactive stories for school-age learners. When you open the site, you start in the Archive view with a 3D globe of Mars and the Moon pinned at the real resting coordinates for three missions: Opportunity and Spirit at Meridiani Planum, the Apollo 11 Descent Stage at Mare Tranquillitatis, and the Ingenuity helicopter at Jezero Crater. You can drag the planets around, adjust the sunlight angle with a slider, and pick an issue to open.

Each mission moves through a simple flow on the left sidebar: Archive, Story, Hardware, Games, Drive, and Badges. In the Story view, illustrated comic panels walk through what happened on the surface from the spacecraft's point of view. In the Hardware view, you can spin a 3D model of the machine sitting on lunar or Martian terrain and click numbered pins—like Opportunity's robotic arm, Spirit's locked wheel, or dusty solar arrays—to see how specific parts made discoveries possible. Below that, students jump into two quick activities: a 15-second Spectrometer Scan where you lock crosshairs onto Martian soil to spot hematite "blueberries," and a Signal Delay simulator where you plan a sol of rover driving and wait through real Earth-to-Mars communication lag. Completing challenges unlocks mission badges like Spectral Eye and tracks your progress across all three issues.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Most young students only hear about Mars rovers or Apollo missions through static textbooks or lists of dates, which makes left-behind hardware feel like old space junk. Our goal is to help kids remember why these machines are still sitting on another world. When a student drags a scanner over rocks or deals with communication delay to move a rover, the engineering trade-offs click in a way reading alone never achieves. We want students and teachers to walk away feeling a genuine connection to the machines that kept working until they physically wore out.

How It Is Creative

Instead of building a basic 3D map with pop-up facts or a plain PDF comic, we combined three formats students already enjoy—an interactive 3D planet archive, graphic-novel storytelling, and short hardware mini-games—into one flow. We also built the stories around the physical scars of the equipment itself: for example, showing how Spirit's broken front wheel dragged through the dirt and accidentally uncovered pure white silica, or how Apollo 11 left its golden descent base behind because weight limits meant trading hardware mass for 21.5 kg of Moon rocks.

Tools, Languages, and Software Used
We built the web app using React, TypeScript/JavaScript, and Tailwind CSS, along with Three.js and WebGL for the 3D Moon and Mars globes and interactive hardware models. We used Google AI Studio for coding, testing, and live hosting, GitHub for team version control across separate branches, and Discord and Figma for async coordination and interface design. Coordinates, mission timelines, and reference spacecraft shapes were pulled from NASA Mars Trek, Moon Trek, NASA 3D Resources, and JPL archives, while comic panel artwork was generated with AI image tools and paired with verified historical captions.

Factors Our Team Considered
First, we wanted to be completely honest about what is creative storytelling and what is documented science. Every comic panel includes a clear label stating: "Speech balloons are dramatized. Caption boxes are documented history." Second, we designed for younger attention spans and classroom accessibility by keeping field tests to 15 seconds, adding an audio toggle and language selector, including a sunlight slider to inspect shadowed terrain, and keeping everything lightweight enough to run in a regular browser without downloads. Finally, instead of rushing 20 shallow dots onto a map, we chose to build three deeper episodes so every story had real interactive detail.
